kurz: How the yields of a single debtor differ by term, and what interest rate expectations of the market can be read from them.

bloecke.md:
On 18 September 2026, a two-year German federal bond yielded 3.24%, a five-year one 3.30, a ten-year one 3.52 and a thirty-year one 3.83%. The debtor and the reference date are the same for all four values; they differ only in their term. If you plot these yields against the remaining maturity, you get the [[Yield curve|yield curve]].

Creditworthiness, currency and trading day are held constant. Only then does the shape show the influence of the term on the interest rate alone. When a German bond is compared with an Italian one, term and default risk become mixed up. The difference in creditworthiness is measured by the yield spread; the curve does not capture it.

The curve results from today's market prices for future payments. It concentrates what banks, insurers, pension funds, central banks and investment funds believe they know about the next thirty years. That is why it is used wherever an interest rate expectation is needed, for example in valuing shares, in pricing mortgage and corporate loans and in accounting for pension provisions.

bloecke.unter: Both curves have a normal slope; the German one lies around 1.5 percentage points lower and is strikingly flat between 2 and 5 years.

bloecke.md:
## Three shapes of the curve

A **normal** curve rises from bottom left to top right, so a longer commitment brings a higher yield. This is the historical norm and the situation in September 2026.

With a **flat** curve, there is hardly any difference left between short and long terms. On 18 September 2026 the German curve showed this in the middle section, where only six basis points separated two and five years. Eight additional years of commitment from the two-year to the ten-year point brought 28 basis points, which is little by historical standards.

An **inverted** curve exists when short terms yield more than long ones. This seems paradoxical but can be explained. Inversion almost always arises at the short end. The central bank raises the overnight rate to curb inflation. The short end follows it almost one for one, because the yield on a two-year bond essentially reflects a chain of expected overnight rates. The long end does not follow, because it already prices in the rate cuts that will follow the expected cooling. The curve therefore tips over because the short end is pushed above the long end, and not because long-term investments become unattractive.

This sequence could be observed in 2022. The two-year Bund yield rose by 325 basis points that year, the ten-year yield by only 274. As a result, an inversion began on 22 November 2022 that lasted 459 trading days until 6 September 2024 and reached 0.76 percentage points at its deepest.

bloecke.titel: Steepness of the German curve (10 years minus 2 years)
bloecke.unter: Year-end levels in percentage points, 2026 as of 18 September. Negative values show the inversion phase; since 2024 the curve has had a normal slope, but in 2026 it is considerably flatter again.

bloecke.md:
## Three theories of the term structure

There are three explanations for the shape of the curve, none of which is sufficient on its own.

According to the **expectations theory**, the long-term rate equals the average of the expected short-term rates over the same period. If this were entirely true, it would make no difference to investors whether they tie up their money for ten years or invest it for one year ten times in a row. From this assumption, the [[Forward rate|forward rate]] that the market already sets today can be calculated.

The **liquidity premium theory** adds a premium. Investors who tie up their money for a long time bear the risk that interest rates rise in the meantime and the price falls, and they give up access to their money. In return they demand a [[Term premium|term premium]] that grows with the term. The theory explains why the curve rises on average over the long term even when nobody expects rising interest rates.

The **market segmentation theory** disputes that there is a single market for all terms at all. Life insurers and pension funds have to cover long-term obligations with long-term bonds and buy at the thirty-year end almost regardless of price. Banks and money market funds are active at the short end. In the weaker version, the preferred habitat approach, investors switch segments only in return for sufficient compensation. This explains kinks and bulges in the curve that do not reflect any expectation, and the effect of central bank bond purchase programmes on the shape of the curve.

bloecke.md: The three views do not contradict each other. The consensus in practice is that the central bank determines the short end, expectations the middle, and the term premium and supply the long end. Supply also depends on the government's debt policy.

At this rate, a long investment and a short investment with reinvestment produce the same final wealth. It is therefore a point of indifference and not a forecast.

bloecke.beispiel: 1.0352^10 / 1.0324^2 = 1.3260; its eighth root minus one gives f = 3.59% for the eight years from 2028.

bloecke.titel: Forward rates derived from the Bund curve
bloecke.unter: Two-year spot yield and forward rates derived from the curve, own calculation from Bundesbank yields on 18 September 2026; the reference line shows today's ECB deposit facility rate.

bloecke.md:
€10,000 is to be invested. Ten years at 3.52% gives €14,133. Two years at 3.24% gives €10,658, after which the amount has to be reinvested for the remaining eight years.

Reinvesting only produces the same result if, in two years' time, an eight-year bond yields 3.59%. If its yield is higher, waiting was better; if it is lower, locking in was better.

The curve therefore does not make the decision for the investor. It only makes visible which interest rate development the investor is betting on with each of the two options. The common advice “keep it short until interest rates rise” is not a neutral position either. It bets that interest rates will rise beyond the 3.59% that is already priced in.

The ECB deposit facility rate has been 2.50% since 16 September 2026, and the two-year Bund yield was 3.09% on 13 October 2026. The gap of 59 basis points shows that the market expects the short-term rate over the next two years to be, on average, noticeably above today's level. Part of this gap, however, is due to the term premium. In the market's assessment, the hiking cycle that began in June 2026 is therefore not yet over.

## Inversion as a recession indicator

Among leading indicators, inversion has the best reputation. According to an analysis of the New York Fed's monthly series from 1959, every US recession since 1966 was preceded by an inversion. Historically, the lead time was around six to eighteen months. Conversely, however, not every inversion was followed by a recession. The curve was inverted in 120 of 812 months since 1959, that is around 15% of the time.

The most recent case is also the biggest failure. From November 2022 to November 2024, the US curve was inverted for 25 months on a monthly average basis, at its deepest by 1.71 percentage points. This is the longest inversion in the entire series since 1959. In March and April 2025 the curve was again slightly inverted on a monthly average. As of September 2026, the NBER has not dated a recession. Germany saw a similar pattern; 459 trading days of inversion were followed by sluggish stagnation, but no slump of the kind the indicator suggested.

Part of the explanation lies in the indicator itself. It measures the gap between two interest rates, and this gap can also shrink for reasons that have nothing to do with the business cycle.

bloecke.titel: Recession probability according to the New York Fed's yield curve model
bloecke.unter: Model value for the US, twelve months ahead in each case, for the forecast months November 2026 to August 2027; after the end of the inversion, the value falls to an unremarkable level.

bloecke.md:
Three mistakes are easy to make:

- An inversion is automatically taken to mean a recession. The longest inversion on record, however, ended without a recession.
- Predictive power is confused with a trading signal. Even when the signal is right, six to eighteen months pass in between. Investors who sell immediately on an inversion often miss a long upward phase and also have to find the right time to get back in.
- A model value is taken for a forecast. The 13.9% for August 2027 is the result of a single regression on a single interest rate spread. A value of this order of magnitude does not mean the all-clear. It only shows that nothing special can currently be read from the curve.

Two explanations compete. According to the first, the curve is purely a carrier of information. It bundles the expectations of all market participants, and the bond market is regarded as the market least driven by sentiment. According to the second, the curve itself affects the economy. Banks fund themselves short-term and lend long-term. An inverted curve eliminates the margin on this business, lending becomes more restrictive, and the economy cools. In this reading, the curve predicts a recession and at the same time helps to bring it about.

Both explanations lose explanatory power when the long end is no longer priced freely by the market. Years of large-scale bond purchases by central banks have depressed the term premium. If the long end is held artificially low, the curve inverts more easily without any economic expectation behind it. This is one of the arguments worth taking seriously for the view that the inversion from 2022 to 2024 was a technical rather than an economic false alarm. It cannot be proven, because term premiums are not observable. They are estimated with models, and different models reach different results.

bloecke.titel: Consequences of the current shape of the curve
bloecke.md:
At 3.09% for two years and 3.46% for ten years (13 October 2026), eight additional years of fixed interest are rewarded with 37 basis points a year. This premium is the price of predictability, which you pay or receive depending on which side of the market you are on.

For investors, this means that long terms currently offer little additional return for a lot of price risk. For borrowers, the same curve applies in mirror image. A long fixed-rate period currently costs relatively little extra over a short one.

Whatever its shape, the curve only shows the situation on a reference date. Whether it will still look the same tomorrow cannot be read from it. It shows which interest rate development is contained in prices today.

eintraege.text: The yield applicable today for a specific term. The yield curve is the curve of spot rates.
The rate for a future period derived from two spot rates. It can be traded today and is therefore a price rather than an estimate.
The interest rate set by the central bank for very short periods. It steers the short end of the curve; the long end is formed in the market.

mitnehmen: The yield curve compares yields of the same creditworthiness and currency on a reference date and thus shows the influence of the term on the interest rate alone.
An inversion arises at the short end because the central bank raises interest rates while the long end already prices in future cuts.
Two points on the curve give the forward rate at which waiting and locking in produce the same result. For the Bund curve of 18 September 2026, this is 3.59% for the eight years from 2028.
In the US, every recession since 1966 was preceded by an inversion, but there were also false alarms, the longest from November 2022 to November 2024.
Because of the lead time of six to eighteen months, inversion is not a usable trading signal despite its good predictive power.

begriffe.text: Representation of yields of the same creditworthiness and currency across different remaining maturities on a reference date. If it slopes upwards it is called normal; if it slopes downwards, inverted.
State in which short terms yield more than long ones. It usually arises because the central bank lifts the short end while the long end prices in future cuts.
Additional yield that investors demand for a longer commitment and the associated interest rate risk. It cannot be observed directly and can only be estimated with models.
Rate for a future period derived from two points on the yield curve. At this rate, short-term investment with reinvestment and a long-term commitment produce the same final wealth.
Weaker form of market segmentation. According to it, investors have a preferred maturity segment and leave it only in return for sufficient compensation.
